newsitem.title: USA: May manufacturing jump rattles markets.
newsitem.headline: May manufacturing jump rattles markets.

text.p: An unexpectedly strong rise in manufacturing activity during May, reported Monday by national purchasing managers, rattled financial markets by raising doubts the economy was slowing as much as had been thought.

Stock and bond markets weakened after the National Association of Purchasing Management reported its index, which measures the pace of manufacturing, jumped to 57.1 percent last month from 54.2 percent in April.
Any reading over 50 percent points to an expanding manufacturing sector.

The apparent pickup in manufacturing overshadowed two government reports that pointed to a second-quarter slowing in national economic activity -- a hoped-for development that analysts said was needed to ward off potential interest-rate rises.

The Commerce Department said consumer spending barely edged up 0.1 percent in April -- the smallest increase since an identical 0.1 percent gain last September -- while personal incomes similarly advanced just 0.1 percent.
That pulls some buying punch out of markets, since consumer spending fuels about two-thirds of national economic activity.
In a separate report, Commerce said spending on new construction projects dropped 1 percent in April to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $596.9 billion, its first monthly decline since December.

But attention centred on the report of rising manufacturing activity. Some economists worried it might portend a summer rebound rather than a continued slowdown from the first quarter's soaring 5.8 percent annual rate.
On the New York Stock Exchange, the Dow Jones industrial index tumbled 41.64 points Monday to close at 7,289.40.

Bond prices fell after the stronger-than-expected NAPM index was published but by the end of the session had regained most of their losses with the bellwether 30-year bond priced to yield 6.90 percent, down from 6.91 percent Friday.
Weaker growth is considered vital to persuade Federal Reserve policy-makers not to raise interest rates in coming months in order to slow the economy by increasing the cost of credit.

"The overall picture in May as indicated by an increase in the growth rates of new orders, backlog of orders, and a continued reduction in prices is one of continued growth in manufacturing activity," said Norbert Ore, chairman of the NAPM's Business Survey Committee and director of purchasing at Sonoco Products Co.

Economist David Jones at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. in New York said the bounce upward in orders was potentially telling, as was a lengthening in supplier delivery times that showed factories were busy.

Jones said the implications might be that "we only saw a pause in the economy in the March-April period and will certainly see a rebound in output and therefore in employment and incomes in the months ahead."
Purchasing managers reported little pressure from rising prices, a positive development in view of the quickened pace of activity since it means inflation remains quiescent.
"The rate of growth of new orders is strong while prices are receding, with only five industries reporting that they are paying higher prices," Ore said.

The easing in consumer spending during April was widely anticipated since earlier reports had shown weaker retail store sales and lackluster new-car demand. Most analysts said it meant slower second-quarter economic expansion might keep the Fed on hold on interest rates.

"It's true that the manufacturing sector is very strong, but the key factor for the Fed is the strength of consumer demand," said David Kelly, managing director for Primark Decision Economics Inc. in Boston.
He said some industries, caught by surprise by the surge in first-quarter demand, likely were rebuilding their stocks of goods early in the second quarter but then might slow down production.

"Manufacturing had some catch-up to do in terms of rebuilding," Kelly said, "But the key is what the consumer is likely to do in future, not what he's already done, and on that score it doesn't look too frightening."
